overview: Cuba’s history lives in household objects as well as public events. Wooden tools, discarded dishes, readers at work and music shared between generations reveal different kinds of knowledge. The examples below distinguish particular communities and periods across the island’s changing political history.

periods.title: Indigenous communities before Spanish colonisation
periods.summary: Los Buchillones was occupied before 1220 and continued into the seventeenth century. This opening marks a selected archaeological window, not the beginning or disappearance of Cuba’s Indigenous peoples.

periods.title: Spanish colonial settlement
periods.summary: Spanish colonisation began in 1511. Colonial institutions and coerced labour transformed the island, while Indigenous people and their descendants survived.

periods.title: British occupation of Havana
periods.summary: British forces captured Havana in 1762 and held it for eleven months before Spain recovered the city. Occupation of Havana did not mean Britain governed the whole island.

periods.title: Spanish rule and expanding sugar plantations
periods.summary: After Spain recovered Havana, sugar production expanded, especially in the nineteenth century. Plantation wealth depended heavily on the labour of enslaved Africans.

periods.title: Independence struggles and emancipation
periods.summary: The Ten Years’ War began in 1868 and ended in 1878 without independence. Slavery finally ended in 1886, and another independence war began in 1895.

periods.title: Spanish withdrawal and U.S. occupation
periods.summary: Spain relinquished sovereignty after the 1898 war. U.S. occupation followed, rather than immediate Cuban control of government.

periods.title: The republic through changing governments
periods.summary: The U.S. occupation ended on May 20, 1902. The new republic faced U.S. intervention and internal political upheavals. The Platt Amendment’s intervention provisions were repealed in 1934.

periods.title: Batista’s dictatorship
periods.summary: Fulgencio Batista seized power in a military coup in March 1952. His dictatorship faced growing opposition and armed rebellion.

periods.title: Revolution and later Cuban society
periods.summary: Batista’s government fell in 1959, and a revolutionary government led by Fidel Castro took power. This broad phase includes later institutional changes and cultural life; it is not one leader’s lifetime.

sections.title: Discoveries: houses, handles and carved seats

items.text: At Los Buchillones on Cuba’s north coast, archaeologists recovered palm thatch and wooden parts of collapsed buildings. A 2006 study placed occupation before 1220 CE through 1640 or later. One partly excavated structure appeared to stand on pilings over water. The surviving pieces let researchers investigate how homes were built; the precise arrangement of every building is still a matter of reconstruction.

The Los Buchillones wood collection includes axe handles with holes prepared for stone heads, and two grooved fragments interpreted as knife handles. The grooves could hold stone blades. Woodworking supplied the part that fitted a tool to a human hand. The collection combines excavated finds and earlier collected objects, so individual pieces do not all have equally precise find records.

Carved seats called dujos also survive from Los Buchillones. Some were made from a single piece of wood, with sculpted human or animal features and supporting legs. Researchers classify them as ceremonial seats. Their careful carving shows skilled work, but they should not be treated as a sample of every household’s everyday furniture.

sections.title: Toilets, rubbish and traces of leisure

items.text: At Habana 958 in Old Havana, a latrine cut into bedrock held pottery, glass, bones and seeds from the late eighteenth and nineteenth centuries. Excavators distinguished waste left during use from later rubble used to fill it. An old toilet can preserve clues to meals and household possessions. Archaeology sometimes finds its best reading material in very unglamorous places.

Excavations in 1999 and 2000 at El Padre, a nineteenth-century coffee plantation near Madruga, recovered two circular pieces cut from discarded crockery. The report interprets them as game counters. Such small objects offer glimpses of activities beyond imposed plantation work. They do not establish which game was played or who used each piece.

In a tradition traced to nineteenth-century Cuba, a lector read aloud to cigar workers as they worked. Reading brought literature and political information into the workshop. Historian Araceli Tinajero studied newspapers and interviewed readers to investigate the practice. It is a little like sharing an audiobook with the whole workplace, except the person doing the reading is actually there.

In 1881, Cuban physician Carlos Finlay proposed that mosquitoes carried yellow fever between people. The Yellow Fever Board led by Walter Reed confirmed mosquito transmission in 1900. Finlay’s insight helped change how people investigated and prevented the disease. The distinction between proposing an explanation and testing it is part of the story of scientific discovery.

A photograph taken by the Kaweiro Group in 2015 shows a mother and daughter joining other Native families in eastern Cuba for a workshop about local medicinal plants. The Smithsonian included it in its 2018 Taíno exhibition announcement. It records knowledge being discussed across generations and challenges the idea that Indigenous people vanished. The photograph does not establish whether a particular remedy works.

Cassava bread connects Cuban households with a wider Caribbean tradition. UNESCO’s 2024 account describes variations in thickness, texture and flavour across Cuba and four other countries, with skills commonly passed on at home and within communities. Learning to make a familiar food can also mean learning from an older relative or neighbour. There is no single recipe that represents every family.

Rumba combines singing, movement and percussion, with roots in communities including Havana and Matanzas. Instruments can include household or workplace utensils, and the audience joins the exchange through clapping and response. UNESCO’s 2016 account describes children and adults learning through imitation within families and neighbourhoods. A musical education can begin by watching someone nearby and joining in.

Punto brings poetry and melody together. Singers perform ten-line stanzas, sometimes learned in advance and sometimes made up as they sing. UNESCO’s 2017 account describes learning by imitation and workshops in Houses of Culture. Improvising a rhyme while keeping a tune takes practice. It gives thinking on your feet a very musical meaning.

For Las Parrandas in central Cuba, competing neighbourhoods spend months preparing floats, costumes, lights and decorations. UNESCO’s 2018 account even mentions people trying to discover the other side’s surprise before the celebration. The preparations combine craft skills with friendly suspense: imagine keeping a spectacular float secret from the neighbours. Participation and practices vary between communities.

ending.text: Spanish sovereignty ended after the 1898 war, followed by U.S. occupation and the republic in 1902. Batista’s government ended in the 1959 revolution. These political transitions did not end Cuban communities or culture, including Indigenous descendants and traditions shared across generations.
